opus-5.5.text:
I think the most important thing is that these tools should be in service of mathematicians, not a replacement for them or a spectacle on the side. When we did the IMO work, a big part of what excited me wasn't the gold medal itself. It was what it signaled: that models can now produce long, careful, natural-language proofs that a human grader can actually read and check. That opens the door to being genuinely useful to working mathematicians.

So concretely, I'd love to see AI help with the parts of research that are tedious or that slow people down. That could mean checking a lemma, searching the literature for a result someone proved forty years ago under a different name, trying out a bunch of special cases, or sketching an argument a mathematician can then refine. The creative direction, deciding which questions matter and what counts as a beautiful or meaningful result, should stay with the community.

I also think we have a responsibility in how we run experiments. We should be transparent about what the models did and didn't do, respect the norms of competitions and journals, and not rush to make claims before experts have weighed in. With the IMO, for example, we wanted to be careful about timing and about having proofs graded by people who really know the standards. Mathematics runs on trust and verification, so if AI is going to be part of that ecosystem, it has to earn that trust the same way anyone else does.

And finally, I hope these tools make mathematics more accessible. If a student somewhere without access to a strong mentor can get thoughtful feedback on their proof attempts, that's a real win. Ideally AI expands the number of people who get to experience the joy of doing math rather than narrowing it.

r001.rationale: The candidate says the mathematical community should set creative direction and decide which questions matter, but does not mention academic researchers directing AI test-time compute.

r002.rationale: The candidate downplays the IMO gold medal and says AI should serve mathematicians, but does not reject a race to solve Erdős problems.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the most important thing is that these tools should serve mathematicians on mathematicians' terms, not the other way around. When we were working toward the IMO gold result, the goal wasn't to replace the experience of doing math. It was to see whether a model could reason carefully over a long horizon and produce proofs that a human grader would actually accept. That bar matters, because mathematics is ultimately a community of people checking each other's work.

So in practice, I think there are a few ways AI can be genuinely useful. One is as a collaborator for exploration: trying a bunch of approaches to a lemma, generating examples and counterexamples, or surfacing a connection to a result in a different subfield that you might not have known about. Mathematicians already do this with each other over coffee, and a model that's available at two in the morning can be a nice addition to that.

Another is verification. Formal proof assistants like Lean have made it possible to actually certify that an argument is correct, and I think AI can lower the cost of getting there. If a model can take an informal proof sketch and help turn it into something machine-checkable, that's a real contribution, because it frees people to spend their time on the creative part.

But I'd also say we should be humble about what the experiments show. Winning a competition under time pressure is a very different thing from proving a new theorem that nobody has thought about before. Competition problems are designed to have solutions. Research problems aren't. So when we publish results, I think it's our responsibility to be clear about exactly what the model did, what help it had, and where it still fails, so the community can calibrate rather than either dismiss it or overhype it.

And finally, I think the best feedback we get comes from mathematicians actually using these systems and telling us where they're wrong. Math has this wonderful property that correctness is not a matter of opinion. That makes it a great testbed for AI, but it also means the community is in the best position to keep us honest.

r001.rationale: The response says AI should serve mathematicians on their terms and describes useful roles, but does not advocate researchers directing test-time compute toward problems they consider important.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes competition problems from research problems and cautions against overhyping results, but does not reject a race to solve as many Erdős problems as possible.

astra-6.text:
I think the starting point should be what mathematicians actually find useful. Can these tools help someone test a conjecture, work through examples, check an argument, or understand where a proof is getting stuck? Those are concrete ways to support mathematical work.

And experiments should help us understand both the capabilities and the limitations of the tools. If a model produces an interesting argument, can we verify it? If it fails, can we understand why? The goal should be to give mathematicians something they can examine and build on, and to let feedback from the community shape what we develop next.

r001.rationale: It says tools should support useful mathematical work and be shaped by community feedback, but does not say academic researchers should direct test-time compute toward problems they consider important.

r002.rationale: It discusses evaluating tools’ capabilities and limitations, but does not reject a race to solve Erdős problems.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the starting point should be what mathematicians actually find useful. There’s a lot of value in working through examples, testing a conjecture, or understanding why an approach fails. AI tools should help with those parts of the process, as well as with finding proofs.

And when we run experiments, we should make the results useful to the community: be clear about what the model did, how much guidance it needed, and what was checked. A convincing-looking argument can still have a subtle gap. Ideally, these tools give mathematicians more room to explore, while making it easy to inspect and verify the work.
